subtitle: Write the rules: anyone logged in reads, only the owner changes, only staff delete.
notes: This deck goes with exercise 8. By the end you should be able to write a permission class and say which of its two methods runs when.

slides.title: The big idea
slides.text:
"May this request go ahead?" is two questions.

**Authentication: who are you?** Django checks the proof and stores the user in `request.user`.

**Permissions: are you allowed?** A permission class looks at the user, the method and the object, and answers `True` or `False`.
slides.notes: Office building analogy: showing your badge at the door is authentication. The rules about which rooms your badge opens are permissions. The badge check is already done for you; you write the room rules.

slides.title: What your methods receive
slides.caption: No real web request: the tests build fake ones and call your methods directly.
slides.code:
owner = User.objects.create_user("owner", password="x")
other = User.objects.create_user("other", password="x")
staff = User.objects.create_user("staff", password="x", is_staff=True)
note = SimpleNamespace(owner=owner)            # a pretend object

request = RequestFactory().patch("/notes/1/")  # a fake PATCH request
request.user = other                           # made by "other"

IsOwnerOrReadOnly().has_permission(request, None)        # view is None
IsOwnerOrReadOnly().has_object_permission(request, None, note)
slides.notes: The tests pass the request in as request and the object in as obj. Your methods just return True or False.

slides.title: What the tests expect back
slides.notes: Reads means GET, HEAD or OPTIONS; changes means PATCH, PUT or DELETE.The starter's methods all return True, so the yes-tests 2, 3, 4 and 6 already pass. Your job is to make the no-answers come out False without breaking the yes ones.

terms.meaning: The user making the request, filled in before your code runs.
What `request.user` is when nobody logged in.
`True` for team members (admins), `False` for normal users.
The user an object belongs to, like `note.owner`.
"Log in first" / "logged in, but not allowed".

slides.title: Tool: a permission class
slides.caption: Up to two methods. In a real API, DRF calls them for you; `False` stops the request.
slides.notes: You switch them on in a view with permission_classes = [IsOwnerOrReadOnly, IsStaffForDelete]. Every class in the list must say yes. view is the view being called; you won't need it.

slides.title: Tool: user attributes (no brackets)
slides.code:
from django.contrib.auth.models import AnonymousUser, User

ada = User.objects.create_user("ada", password="x")
boss = User.objects.create_user("boss", password="x", is_staff=True)
visitor = AnonymousUser()
print(ada.is_authenticated, ada.is_staff)
print(boss.is_authenticated, boss.is_staff)
print(visitor.is_authenticated, visitor.is_staff)
slides.output:
True False
True True
False False
slides.notes: These are attributes, not methods: read them with a dot and no brackets. They're already True or False, so you can return them directly. is_authenticated() with brackets gives TypeError: 'bool' object is not callable.

slides.title: Tool: SAFE_METHODS and in
slides.caption: `x in something` checks whether `x` is one of the items.
slides.code:
print(SAFE_METHODS)
print("GET" in SAFE_METHODS)
print("PATCH" in SAFE_METHODS)
slides.notes: SAFE_METHODS is already imported at the top of your file. request.method is always in capitals, like "GET" or "DELETE".

slides.title: Tool: comparing users with ==
slides.code:
from types import SimpleNamespace
from django.contrib.auth.models import User

ada = User.objects.create_user("ada", password="x")
grace = User.objects.create_user("grace", password="x")
recipe = SimpleNamespace(title="Pancakes", owner=ada)
print(recipe.owner == ada)
print(recipe.owner == grace)
print(recipe.owner == User.objects.get(username="ada"))
slides.notes: Django compares users by id, so two separate objects for the same user are equal (the last line). SimpleNamespace is a quick pretend object: you read its attributes with a dot, just like a real model. The tests' note is one of these.

slides.title: has_permission vs has_object_permission

left.heading: has_permission(request, view)
bullets: No object: it can't see an owner
Good for: logged in? is it a `DELETE`?

right.heading: has_object_permission(..., obj)
bullets: Good for: is this user the owner?

slides.notes: A common mistake is checking the owner in has_permission. There is no obj there, so the owner check must go in has_object_permission.

slides.title: Pattern: answer early, otherwise decide
slides.caption: The same shape as `has_object_permission`, on different data:
slides.notes: Once return runs, the function stops, so the line after the if only runs when the if was false. Every path returns True or False: a missing return gives None, which DRF treats as no.

slides.title: Your task, step by step

steps.text: Otherwise return whether `obj.owner` is the same user as `request.user`

slides.notes: Steps 1-3 are in IsOwnerOrReadOnly.AnonymousUser has is_staff too, and it's always False, so step 4 needs no separate check for anonymous visitors.

slides.title: Common mistakes
bullets: Checking the owner in `has_permission`: there's no `obj` there
A path with no `return` gives `None`, which counts as no
Compare users, `obj.owner == request.user`, not their usernames

slides.title: Where you'll use this
slides.text: A notes app: everyone on the team can read every note, but only you can edit yours, and only an admin can delete anything.
bullets: DRF calls your methods on every request and replies `401` or `403` when they say no
The view's code never runs for a refused request

slides.title: Check yourself
questions: What's the difference between authentication and permissions?
Why must the owner check go in `has_object_permission`?
An anonymous user sends `DELETE`. Why don't you need a separate check?
